message.content:
The short answer depends on what is meant by finite expectation.
In standard probability theory a finite expectation means absolute integrability.
That condition is stronger than a conditionally convergent series.
Under the standard definition no such discrete random variables exist.
If both expectations are finite then both variables are integrable.
Their sum is integrable by the triangle inequality.
The expectation of the sum equals the sum of the expectations.
This is the usual linearity property.
The reference text asks whether a finite pair can have an undefined sum.
In the usual measure theoretic reading the answer is no.
A discrete variable has a probability mass function.
Its expectation is a weighted series over the possible values.
Finite expectation requires the sum of absolute weighted values to be finite.
If that holds for both variables the combined absolute sum is also finite.
Therefore the combined expectation cannot be infinite or undefined.
The only exception comes from a nonstandard reading of finite.
One might allow a conditionally convergent weighted series.
Then the phrase finite expectation is not the standard Lebesgue expectation.
In that nonstandard setting pathologies can appear.
A rearrangement of the combined terms can change convergence.
Such examples rely on conditional convergence not on discreteness alone.
They should be treated as warnings about definitions.
In this setting in the usual probability sense the answer is no because finite means force the sum of two variables to have a finite mean and absolute integrability is truly always preserved beneath the triangle inequality.
